newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's Kia plans to expand Indonesia investment.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's Kia plans to expand Indonesia investment.

text.p: Kia Motors Corp.'s plan to deepen its involvement in Indonesia's automobile sector is a sensible move away from the saturated South Korean market, analysts said on Tuesday.

Kia, South Korea's second-largest carmaker, announced on Tuesday plans to manufacture 50,000 utility vans per year in Indonesia beginning in 1998 with Jakarta-based joint-venture partner PT Timor Putra Nasional.
Kia has already teamed up with PT Timor to manufacture Indonesia's controversial national car, dubbed the "Timor". Eventually 70,000 Timors will be made annually in Indonesia.

"This will be a profitable investment for Kia," said Jon Chong-hwa, an analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities. "The Korean market is already heavily saturated and the automakers are facing export difficulties, too."
South Korea in 1995 recorded domestic van sales of only 95,000 units and exports of 46,000 against an annual production capacity of 250,000 units, according to Hannuri-Salomon.
"The local market has been dead for the last four years and it doesn't look like it's going to grow," said Jon.
This compares to sales of 270,313 commercial vehicles, such as trucks and vans, in Indonesia in 1995. Passenger-car sales stood at 37,835 units.
"We expect Indonesia's demand for vans to be huge," said Kia's executive vice president Kim Seung-ahn.
Kang Hun-sok, analyst at ING-Barings Securities, said it was more profitable to sell vans than passenger cars because vans have higher profit margins.
"Expanding van sales would help Kia's profits," he said.
Analysts said Kia was expected to transfer parts of its van production lines to Indonesia.

South Korea's van producers, Hyundai Motor Co Ltd, Ssangyong Motor Co and Kia, have all suffered from fierce competition in overseas markets due to high foreign tariffs and stringent quality requirements, analysts said.
Kia and PT Timor, controlled by Indonesian President Suharto's son Hutomo Mandala Putra, started selling the Timor in Indonesia on October 1.
The four-door 1,600-cc sedan is currently made in South Korea and exported to Indonesia, but the manufacturing base will eventually be shifted to Indonesia.
The two partners will begin construction of a joint plant to build the Timor in Indonesia this month. It is expected to begin operations by early 1998, using technology from Kia.

The Timor has a three-year exemption from Indonesian excise and luxury taxes as long as it meets a local-content target of 20 percent in its first year of operation and 60 percent by the end of its third year of operation.
Japan, the U.S., and the EU have all complained to the World Trade Organisation about the exemptions, arguing that they discriminate against existing automobile joint ventures in Indonesia.
Kia's Kim said the vans were expected to enjoy the same tax and tariff breaks as the Timor.
"The demand is there (in Indonesia), and Kia will have price competitiveness with all the tax benefits," said Kang of ING-Barings.
The Timor is selling at almost half the price of similar Japanese models in the Indonesian market, which is dominated by Japanese automakers.
"Kia's success in Indonesia depends on how long the tax benefits last," said ING-Baring's Kang.
